title: Promoting Fairness and Priority in Selecting k-Winners Using IRV

problem.claim: The paper addresses selecting winners from ranked ballots so that group priority is satisfied and each group receives a representative winner.

gap.claim: Original user preferences may need modification to satisfy fairness and priority requirements.

contributions.claim: The paper formalizes the margin-finding problem under preference modification.
The paper studies IRV as a preference aggregation method for fairness- and priority-aware winner selection and compares it with positional methods.
The paper provides hardness results and algorithms with theoretical guarantees, while investigating efficiency opportunities.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report exhaustive experiments across multiple applications and large-scale datasets.
The authors report that the experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of IRV and the qualitative and scalability-wise efficacy of their solutions.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames winner selection from ranked ballots submitted by many users.
The selection must respect protected-group priority and choose a representative winner for each group.
Meeting these fairness and priority requirements may require modifying the original preferences.
The paper evaluates IRV, develops formal and algorithmic results, and investigates efficiency.
The authors report experiments on multiple applications and large-scale datasets.

source_observation.claim: The paper reports that IRV has advantages over positional methods for the considered preference aggregation setting.

interpretation.claim: The choice of aggregation rule can materially affect the feasibility or quality of fairness- and priority-aware selection.

application.claim: Compare aggregation mechanisms under the specific fairness and priority constraints of the target selection task.

exception.claim: The abstract does not identify which applications, datasets, or metrics establish the reported advantages.

unknowns: The abstract does not state the exact hardness results or complexity assumptions.
The abstract does not describe the algorithms, guarantees, or efficiency techniques in detail.
The abstract does not specify the experimental applications, datasets, metrics, baselines, or numerical results.
The abstract does not define the cost or constraints of preference modifications.
